title: UNH student organizations celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month with campus-wide events - The Charger Bulletin
content: Hispanic Heritage Month is underway, and student organizations across campus are preparing cultural, artistic and community-centered events. From silent discos to animation displays, resident student organizations (RSOs) are highlighting Hispanic culture, honoring community traditions and bringing students together. The Myatt Center for Diversity and Inclusion anchors the programming each year, but this fall, student-led organizations are taking an especially active role. The Latin American Student Association (LASA), the university’s Animation Club and Greek-letter organizations are collaborating to create one of the most event-packed calendars the university has seen in recent years. A LASA official said that Hispanic Heritage Month is more than a celebration; it is about unity, identity and honoring people who shape Hispanic culture. In a statement given by LASA president Nikki Rosario, a senior marine biology student, and vice president Steven Ojeda, a junior psychology student with a focus in forensics, said: “Hispanic Heritage Month is not just about celebrating one culture but about celebrating our different identities while recognizing what brings us together. We want our members and everyone who attends our events to feel seen, understood, and proud to be part of such a beautiful culture,” they said. “El Apagon represents what LASA is about: Bringing people together through culture and community.” The students said “El Apagon” is one of their favorite events this year, inspired by Bad Bunny’s song and the blackout scene in the 2021 movie, “In the Heights.” Both references use darkness as a symbol of community resilience, something LASA members say they hope to bring to campus. The Animation Club will co-host LA Animación de Cultura with LASA on Oct. 6, focusing on Hispanic representation in animation. Animation Club president Gian Rodriguez, a senior graphic & digital design student, shared why this event matters. “As a Mexican and Puerto Rican student, it is amazing to see fellow Hispanic animators mold and shape what Hispanic culture is in animation,” he said. The event will explore both positive representation and harmful stereotypes in animated media. Students will also have the chance to create their own character inspired by Hispanic Culture. “We feel it is important to showcase and talk about the involvement of culturally rich communities in animation, as they are part of the beauty that helps make such captivating pieces of media,” Rodriguez said. Students will have opportunities to engage with art, music, film, dance and cultural education all led by organizations committed to uplifting Hispanic voices. From LASA’s community-centered programming to the Animation Club’s creative showcase, this year’s Hispanic Heritage Month events highlight the diversity, resilience and joy of Hispanic culture at the university. title: Food Among the Trees - University of New Hampshire
content: ‌New Hampshire is more than 80% forested, second ‌in coverage only to Maine in the U.S. The Adaptive ‌Agroforestry Principles and Teaching (ADAPT) program is leveraging this important resource through the testing and teaching of agroforestry concepts and methods, work that will support local farming and sustain a stronger regional food system. Agroforestry expands agricultural opportunities by embracing, rather than seeking to overcome, the tree-filled landscape. ADAPT is a collaborative effort led by Heidi Asbjornsen, professor of natural resources and the environment, that also includes researchers at Yale University, Dartmouth College, and 12 operating farms. ADAPT works with three primary types of agroforestry. Forest farming grows shade-tolerant crops under an existing tree canopy. Food forests contain food-producing plants of varying heights, such as nut trees, berry bushes, and herbs, within the same space. And silvopasture provides livestock pasturing and grazing space among trees. Unlike most fully cleared pasture and crop lands, all offer welcoming habitats for beneficial insects, pollinators, and wildlife. “Agroforestry can increase crop diversity and sustainability, providing farmers and growers with more resilience in changing conditions as well as expanding income-generating opportunities,” says Asbjornsen. “But agroforestry systems are complex to manage. Education and extension are critical parts of ADAPT so that we can share our research-based insights with the community.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Counting the Recovery of New Hampshire Bats - University of New Hampshire
content: New Hampshire bats have been in crisis for years. Beginning in 2009, a fatal fungal disease known as white-nose syndrome devastated all five of the state’s cave-hibernating bat species. Researchers and Extension specialists in COLSA are now teaming up with the NH Fish and Game Department and Granite State landowners to support one of the state’s key programs supporting the conservation and recovery of the remaining bat populations: NH Bat Counts. Laura Kloepper, associate professor of biological sciences, leads UNH’s Ecological Acoustics and Behavior Lab, studying how animals use acoustics to navigate the world and how we, in turn, can use acoustics to monitor them. Acoustic technology has gotten both better and less expensive in recent years, and it can now be applied to NH Bat Counts. “NH Bat Counts has been active for a long time, and we’re joining it now to contribute our experience with advanced technology to expand and improve data gathering,” says Kloepper. “The work is vital for tracking bat abundance and providing insights to protect them and their habitats.” Why do bats matter to us? Estimates vary, but studies indicate bats contribute at least $3.7 billion and potentially more than $50 billion in insect pest control for U.S. agriculture alone every year. Without them, controlling pests becomes more costly and losses for New Hampshire industries such as agriculture and forestry increase. White-nose syndrome was first detected in hibernating bats in New York State in 2006. When it arrived in New Hampshire in 2009, surveys of the four largest caves and mines favored by bats for hibernation counted 3,230 of these flying mammals. By 2011, that number had plummeted to 16. For reasons that remain poorly understood, some species of bats elsewhere have proven to be more resilient to the fungus that causes white-nose syndrome. And some colonies are beginning to grow once again, though their numbers remain much smaller than pre-disease. “There has been growth in some of the maternity colonies over the last few years,” says Haley Andreozzi ’13G, Extension state specialist and Extension professor of wildlife conservation. “In 2022, we had a colony with more than 700 individuals, the first time we’ve measured one that large. There’s a long way to go — pre-disease, some colonies had thousands of bats — but we’re beginning to see some small but needed wins for the bats.” The NH Fish and Game Department, NH Audubon, and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service launched NH Bat Counts in 2012 to find and quantify the survivors. The program monitors summer bat colonies in barns, attics, steeples, and other structures where female bats gather and give birth to their young during the warmer months. NH Bat Counts is now spearheaded by Sandra Houghton ’04G, wildlife diversity biologist with the NH Fish and Game Department, and Andreozzi. Houghton and Andreozzi have worked together to extend and formalize the program over the past half dozen years. “The data from NH Bat Counts volunteers furthers our knowledge about the location, species, and status of bat colonies in New Hampshire,” says Houghton. “It helps us prioritize conservation efforts while also creating a network of bat ambassadors.” Kloepper’s work will make it possible to look at trends in the acoustic energy produced by the bats to get a sense of movement within the colonies, the timing of pup independence, how environmental conditions such as weather impact pup emergence and roost shifting, and more. The recorders will also allow volunteers to obtain nightly population estimates far more efficiently than previously possible. Andreozzi notes the interest and enthusiasm of the volunteers, who enjoy learning about how valuable their barns and other structures are for bats and contributing to the efforts to protect bat colonies. Now, Kloepper’s expertise and recorder technologies will enable the volunteers to help even more. She has also involved her students in the research and outreach efforts, and eight undergraduates have formed a “bat count” team devoted to devising better ways to count bats for conservation. “It’s a great example of how research is being done at UNH,” says Kloepper. “All parties — researchers, students, Extension, and state experts — are out in the New Hampshire community, working together toward a common goal.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: Chipotle Opens Near UNH in Durham, New Hampshire - hoodline.com
content: Chipotle Mexican Grill is planting a new flag steps from the University of New Hampshire campus, with a restaurant planned at 7 Mill Road, Suite A, in Durham on Sept. 29, 2026. It follows an Aug. 19 opening in Braintree, Massachusetts, marking a fresh push by the burrito chain into the Boston-Manchester corridor. The Durham location sits near the UNH campus, according to Boston Real Estate Times. The Braintree restaurant, at 165 Pearl St., opened Aug. 19, giving Chipotle two fresh footholds in the region within about six weeks of each other. UNH provides a substantial nearby campus backdrop, though its degree-seeking enrollment in Durham dipped from 13,360 in fall 2024 to 12,819 in fall 2025. The university also said it received 2,471 first-year deposits for fall 2026, nearly 4% more than a year earlier. The figures offer a snapshot of the student population close to the new restaurant, without indicating how many students will become customers. UNH’s Durham enrollment history and fall 2026 admissions update provide the counts. The Durham address falls within Durham Landing, a retail property marketed by Eastern Retail as having 10,700 square feet of existing endcap space and redeveloped small-shop units ranging from 1,730 to 7,885 square feet, subdividable to fit different tenants. Eastern Retail's listing describes the property as ideal for full-service and quick-service restaurants, along with fitness and medical uses, suggesting Chipotle is one of several types of businesses the site was built to attract. Durham's own planning records point to a larger redevelopment underway in the same area. A site-plan page on the town's website identifies a Mill Plaza project at 5 Mill Road involving architectural improvements to the building facade and other exterior renovations, with 5-7 Mill Road LLC listed as the property owner. A separate site-plan review application on file with the town references 7 Mill Road, Unit L, as part of that broader Mill Plaza redevelopment, which the filing describes as including 108 residential units, 258 beds, and roughly 80,250 square feet of total commercial space once complete. The Mill Plaza property has a longer planning history distinct from the current restaurant opening. In 2022, Durham’s Planning Board denied a redevelopment application for Mill Plaza, and the state Housing Appeals Board affirmed that decision later that year. Town records identify 5 and 7 Mill Road as being in Durham’s Central Business zoning district. That history puts the new storefront within a site that has previously drawn formal land-use review, but does not establish that Chipotle’s tenancy was part of the earlier proposal. The town’s account of the 2022 denial and its update on the appeal document those decisions. Both the Braintree and Durham restaurants are expected to create employment opportunities in the region, and Chipotle is hiring for both, with each location carrying approximately 30 open positions, per the same report. Once open, both restaurants are set to run daily from 10:45 a.m. to 10 p.m., the outlet reports. The expansion adds to Chipotle's presence in the broader Boston and New Hampshire markets, as the chain continues building out its footprint across the region. The two local openings also come amid a wider company expansion. Chipotle ended 2025 with 4,056 restaurants and opened 334 company-owned locations that year, while comparable restaurant sales fell 1.7%. The company forecast 350 to 370 new openings in 2026. The figures place the Braintree and Durham restaurants within a national growth push, even as the chain reported a year-over-year decline in sales at established locations. Chipotle’s 2025 results and 2026 outlook give the companywide totals. Chipotle is also promoting new and limited-time menu offerings across the Boston-Manchester region, including pollo asado, a grilled chicken option seasoned with garlic and Mexican spices and finished with cilantro and citrus, alongside chili lime chips seasoned with lime and chili peppers. The chain is pairing that with a high-protein menu for the market, featuring items ranging from 15 to 81 grams of protein, such as a double high-protein bowl, a high protein-high fiber bowl, and a high-protein cup, plus a single chicken taco starting at $3.50. Chipotle Rewards members can also tap into monthly food rewards and customizable birthday benefits, while new members can receive free chips and guac with a purchase. The chain additionally offers family meal options built for groups eating at home, and local organizations can use Chipotle's fundraising program, which helps groups raise money for community causes through restaurant-based fundraising events. For the roughly 60 workers Chipotle hopes to hire across the two new restaurants, the company points to a broader benefits package. Employees are eligible for a crew bonus program that can provide the chance to earn an additional month's pay each year, along with a debt-free college degree program. Workers also have access to English-as-a-second-language support, and employees and their families can access mental health care, according to the same report. title: What Are UNH Stock Investors Betting On? - trefis.com
content: UnitedHealth (UNH) stock trades at 22.5 times its past year’s adjusted earnings, which are normalized net income with stock-based pay added back. That multiple leaves little room for error after three years of shrinking operating margins, sitting near the stock’s 10-year median despite fundamentally weaker profitability. But the price looks different against the profit expected for fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027. So what are UnitedHealth investors betting on? UnitedHealth investors are betting on wider margins in fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027. A P/E is the share price divided by a year of profit. On the consensus forecast for fiscal 2026, today’s price is 19.0 times earnings. On the fiscal 2027 forecast, it is 16.8 times, beside 22.5 times for the past year. The consensus forecast has profit rising 12.9% from fiscal 2026 to fiscal 2027. Sales in the forecast rise just 3.0% over the same year. Profit only outgrows sales when a company keeps more of each dollar of sales. So the forecast P/Es are real only if UnitedHealth’s net margin widens—an expansion that ultimately depends on reversing the slide in its operating margins. Not over the last three years. Operating margin is the share of sales left after medical and running costs. At UnitedHealth, it fell each year, from 8.8% three years ago to 4.8% now. UnitedHealth’s margins did widen in the second quarter of fiscal 2026. Operating earnings grew 55% from a year earlier on flat revenue. Management credited product and portfolio changes, and said better results in Medicare Advantage put its UnitedHealthcare business ahead of expectations. Medical costs that quarter were also flattered by $860 million in favorable reserve adjustments—mostly developed from earlier in 2026—giving a substantial one-time boost to that 55% operating jump. Management then raised its fiscal 2026 guidance for adjusted earnings per share to $19.50 to $20. The consensus forecast of $19.95 per share for fiscal 2026 is near the top of that guidance. Management called that range the right baseline to build toward its long-term earnings growth goal of 13% to 16%. The forecast’s fiscal 2027 profit growth is at about the low end of that goal. So the forecast sits close to management’s own targets, at the upper end for fiscal 2026. Mostly in medical costs, starting with UnitedHealth’s commercial benefits business. Management said commercial costs are stubbornly high and rising above expectations. Management also moved the full recovery of commercial margins past 2027. If those costs do not ease, the consensus forecast for fiscal 2027 profit is more likely to fall than rise. Medicare Advantage is the other major risk, despite driving the second quarter’s beat. Management said its own changes to benefits, care management and networks were a primary reason Medicare costs grew less than expected. Management added that the slower growth is not a turning point, and that Medicare costs are continuing at high levels. If Medicare cost growth speeds up again, fiscal 2027 profit could fall short of the consensus forecast. The medical care ratio is the share of premiums UnitedHealth spends on care. Management expects it at 88.1% for fiscal 2026, plus or minus a quarter of a percentage point. UnitedHealth reports its third quarter on October 13, 2026. Management said it would probably update its Medicare cost estimate then. If UnitedHealth’s margins recover as the forecast assumes, the P/Es on the consensus forecast are a fair picture of today’s price. Commercial medical costs are the likeliest place for that recovery to fall short. Management has already pushed back the commercial margin recovery. If those costs stay high, the stock is riskier than it looks. At current levels, you are paying for margin recovery before it has fully materialized. An upward revision to the 2026 medical care ratio in the October report would indicate that this recovery is taking longer than projected. Before you decide on UNH, consider a better choice. title: Marlborough’s Ava VanBuskirk finds her footing playing soccer at University of New Hampshire - Community Advocate
content: Ava VanBuskirk (Ryan Moran/University of New Hampshire) DURHAM, NH – AUGUST 12: UNH Women’s Soccer hosts the 2026 Media Day at the UNH Field House on August 12, 2026 in Durham, New Hampshire. (Photo by Alex Miller) Ava VanBuskirk during her time in Marlborough (Photo/Jesse Kucewicz) Ava VanBuskirk during her time in Marlborough (Photo/Jesse Kucewicz) MARLBOROUGH – Sarah Casey’s path to becoming Marlborough Hig… MARLBOROUGH – Every year, Meredith Harris parks at Kelleher … Ava VanBuskirk (Ryan Moran/University of New Hampshire) MARLBOROUGH – When Ava VanBuskirk left Marlborough High School with 100-plus career goals, she hoped her success in finding the back of the net would continue at her next stop: the University of New Hampshire. Her freshman year, she played 41 minutes. She played 65 minutes in her sophomore year, but injuries to both knees cut her season short and required separate surgeries. She spent five months rehabbing only to play 10 minutes of the Wildcats’ final spring game. But those 10 minutes were plenty to show her enormous potential. “She made a huge impact on the team in those 10 minutes,” head coach Steve Welham told the Community Advocate. “It was awesome to see. Ava has carried that impact into this season.” In the team’s first four games this fall, VanBuskirk averaged 37 minutes but didn’t figure in any of the team’s goals. Then, over three days, she scored her first two collegiate goals in a 4-1 win over Northeastern, followed by another goal in a 4-2 win over Merrimack. DURHAM, NH – AUGUST 12: UNH Women’s Soccer hosts the 2026 Media Day at the UNH Field House on August 12, 2026 in Durham, New Hampshire. (Photo by Alex Miller) “Ava has been a very positive story for us,” said Welham. “She has developed each year and is taking this opportunity and really running with it. She can fly – she has a great engine, great endurance, and she’s just really coming into her own.” The rehabilitation process was hardly sunshine and rainbows for VanBuskirk. “It was hard mentally. I had never been a player who was on the sidelines to watch. That was a big transition going from always playing and soccer always being my outlet, and then not having that,” said VanBuskirk, an aspiring elementary school teacher. “My teammates were awesome and always included me. It was about finding my role on the team in a different way. … I took the role of being on the bench and cheering as loud as I could.” VanBuskirk went to physical therapy three times a week and worked with different trainers to regain her strength and mobility. Those grueling workouts are now paying off. She’s been electric on the field, said Welham. “She’s two-footed. She loves to go 1-versus-1 on a defender,” he said. “She’s technical, she’s dynamic, and her game is built around pace and dynamic movement on and off the ball. Her energy and positivity coming off the bench have just elevated the team to another level.” Ava VanBuskirk during her time in Marlborough (Photo/Jesse Kucewicz) Her first collegiate goal – a rebound off an initial shot taken by Elizabeth Finn – was “such a surreal feeling,” she said. At the time of the score, VanBuskirk was focused on getting back on the field; scoring was simply an added bonus. “I was really focusing on coming back from my injury and trying to get back to where I was before, so when I got my opportunity to get on the field and play, I took it and did my best,” VanBuskirk said. “Instead of stressing myself out, I focused on having fun and why I play the sport. It really helped that the girls around me supported me and were excited for me, along with my family, friends, and coaches.” Thirteen minutes after her first collegiate goal, VanBuskirk scored another. Each time, her “large soccer family” – including her mother Pam, a Marlborough soccer alum; her brother Joey; and her aunt, uncle, and cousin, who all played collegiately – were there to celebrate in the stands. Ava VanBuskirk during her time in Marlborough (Photo/Jesse Kucewicz) “Soccer has always been a part of my life,” VanBuskirk said. “I looked up to my brother and older cousins, and we played soccer on every family outing and summer trip, always with a soccer ball. It was nice being able to grow up with everyone, especially my brother, because he’s always been my biggest role model, and I always wanted to make him proud.” Unlock the power of local outreach with our platform! title: Giant pumpkins grow from Durham retirement community project with UNH - Foster's Daily Democrat
content: DURHAM — Giant pumpkins were grown by residents of Brookdale Spruce Wood, a retirement community, and one will be entered in the Deerfield Fair. The community project brought together people from Brookdale Spruce Wood, the University of New Hampshire, families, friends and neighbors, resulting in five very big pumpkins. The Brookdale Spruce Wood UNH giant pumpkin project began in 2025, when a photograph of an enormous pumpkin caught residents' attention during a presentation about “Our Backyard” by resident Jim Cross, 79, an outdoor enthusiast and nature lover. Inspired by the image, Cross and fellow resident, friend and outdoor partner-in-crime Daniel Reich, 86, began researching how to grow a giant pumpkin of their own. Their efforts led them to Christopher Hernandez, assistant professor of plant breeding at the University of New Hampshire. With his guidance, Cross and Reich laid out and rototilled three pumpkin patches. They then made 10 trips to Coyote Spring Farm in Lee to haul horse manure back to the patches. With Hernandez's help, they obtained seeds from two prize-winning pumpkins, including one grown in 2018 by Steve Geddes of Boscawen that weighed 2,528 pounds (a U.S. record for six years). On June 5, Cross, Reich and Hernandez planted four pumpkin seedlings – initially grown by UNH students – in each of the three pumpkin patches surrounding Brookdale Spruce Wood. Geddes donated retired paper-mill conveyor-belt squares to serve as sturdy “beds” for the pumpkins. He and Hernandez also taught the team about support and cushioning, including the use of sand and pool noodles. Old sheets provided shade and protection from the sun. Cross and Reich tended the plants every day and with Hernandez's guidance, the team narrowed the field to the two strongest plants in each patch and carefully assisted with pollination. Over the next 16 weeks, throughout July, August and September, the once-tiny seeds/seedlings grew rapidly. The project soon attracted attention beyond Brookdale Spruce Wood. Members of the New Hampshire Giant Pumpkin Association paid the community a visit. Neighbors from the surrounding community stopped by during their daily walks to check on the pumpkins, while visiting family and friends did the same. Those regular visits sparked conversations and new friendships. The largest pumpkin, affectionately named “Frankenstein,” reached an impressive 1,000 pounds before splitting open! Despite the major disappointment, the project continued. Brookdale Spruce Wood residents helped name the four remaining pumpkins: The group plans to officially weigh the pumpkins on Wednesday, Sept. 30. The winning pumpkin will be sent to the Deerfield Fair to compete on Thursday, Oct. 1 against approximately 30 other pumpkins in the heaviest giant-pumpkin and/or prettiest giant-pumpkin competition.

title: New poll shows Gov. Phil Scott leading Amanda Janoo by 10 points - VTDigger
content:
Prepare for Vermont’s Nov. 3 general election with VTDigger’s 2026 Election Guide. Get the latest reporting from towns across Vermont delivered each morning in Daily Digger, our free newsletter. Gov. Phil Scott holds a 10-point lead over progressive Democrat Amanda Janoo in a poll released Monday, a striking reversal from a separate survey last week that showed the race in a statistical tie. Vermont Public’s 2026 Poll reported Scott is leading Janoo by 10 points, 42% to 32%. These results reflect a 16-point swing from Friday’s Green Mountain State Poll by the University of New Hampshire, which, based on margin of error in the survey, declared a “statistical tie,” with Janoo leading the race 49% to 43%. “Public polling has always undervalued the Governor’s support,” Scott’s campaign spokesperson Emma Shouldice wrote in a statement Monday. She added that the Vermont Public poll was “much better” than the UNH survey, but still discounted Scott. Among likely voters — the Vermonters polled who said they would “definitely” or “probably vote” — the margin remained 10 points with the incumbent Scott leading 44% to 34%. Sixteen percent of those likely voters remain unsure or have no opinion, according to the poll. Vermont Public’s poll also reported former Democratic Lt. Gov. Molly Gray leading Republican incumbent John Rodgers by eight points in the lieutenant governor race. U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt. is leading the congressional race against Republican nominee Gerald Malloy, 43% to 28%. Longtime Vermont political journalist Chris Graff called last week’s UNH poll an “outlier.” “I think the Vermont Public poll is a little more in line with how those of us who follow this closely see the race, which is that Governor Scott maintains a lead,” he said in an interview Monday. “Amanda Janoo has a strong following but is largely unknown.” Scott remained the most popular governor in the country as of a July report by the firm Morning Consult. Vermont Public’s polling reported that Scott held a 45% approval rating, a 15-point decline since their last poll in 2022. UNH also reported a 47% approval rating, which had decreased by five points since July. Graff said that declining approval ratings are to be expected for Scott, but that the drop could be explained by Scott not having “solved the problems that are facing the state of Vermont.” Alternatively, he said, Scott’s ratings could be explained by national sentiment. “The national mood is such that if you have an ‘R’ beside your name — even if you’re someone like Phil Scott — that ‘R’ is an anchor,” Graff said. Twenty percent is a significant number of uncertain voters this close to the election, Graff said. He expects that debates will “make a difference,” but that Janoo doesn’t have the “money or organization” to reach the “larger number of voters” across the state who are undecided. “We haven’t seen (the candidates debate) yet,” Graff said. “She is not yet defined in the public. People haven’t seen her in person, so I think she was able to beat Aly Richards by being the candidate of change, and really electrifying that base, but it was a very narrow win. Now in a general election, you have a far, far larger number of voters you have to reach.” Scott’s team remains confident that he and Vermonters are on the same page, Shouldice wrote. “What we are certain of is that Vermonters share the Governor’s frustration on affordability issues and that’s why we’re focused on getting commonsense legislators elected that will work with him to lower property taxes, housing, healthcare and energy costs,” she wrote. Janoo, an economist, had never run for office and was relatively unknown before her grassroots campaign. She also remains optimistic about November’s election, according to a Monday press release. “This is going to be a close race but no matter what,” she wrote, “I’m incredibly proud of the way we’re bringing people together to celebrate the things we love about where we live, to invite people to articulate the Vermont we want for our children and grandchildren and to recognize together, we have everything we need to get there.” VTDigger's intern.

(WHDH) - Lindsay Clancy will be back in court Tuesday for a hearing regarding several motions in the murder case against her. Clancy’s Defense Attorney Kevin Reddington will argue there was never enough evidence to convict Clancy. In Clancy’s inital trial, his defense was built on claims that she was mentally ill, and did not know right from wrong when she strangled her three young children in January 2023. Judge Michael Sullivan agreed to hear arguments on a motion asking him to dismiss the case based on Double Jeopardy. The defense claims the lone holdout juror refused to follow his instructions regarding reasonable doubt. Reddington also has a third motion, asking the judge to investigate the holdout juror, examine data on his cell phone, and provide him with juror notes and transcripts of sidebar discussions. An attorney for the holdout juror spoke to Fox News’ Kayleigh McEnany. “Kevin Reddington is clearly attacking the Sixth Amendment,” said Edward Paltzik, attorney for the holdout juror. “He’s clearly attacking the right to trial by jury. He is off the rails.” Paltzik said his client does not doubt Clancy’s guilt. He said his client’s focus remains on the victims, Cola, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months. “It’s about three innocent children who were murdered by their demonic mother,” Paltzik said. “And this shouldn’t be controversial. We are not backing down. We’re not giving one inch.” A retired judge who has presided over that same courtroom said Reddington’s motions face legal hurdles. “It’s problematic on several fronts,” said Christopher Muse, a retired Plymouth County Superior Court Judge. “In part because a Massachusetts judge has discretion to decide whether a juror inquiry is warranted and the Supreme Judicial Court has already declined to step in and overrule Judge Sullivan’s decision to declare a mistrial.” In an exclusive 7NEWS/University of New Hampshire Survey Center poll, nearly 600 Massachusetts residents were asked about the Clancy case. Forty-three percent said they believe prosecutors should definitely or probably should retry Clancy. Thirty-three percent said definitely or probably should not, while 24 percent said they don’t know or have no opinion. Among those who’ve heard about the case, 40 percent said they believe Clancy is guilty, 36 percent said they believe she is not guilty, and 24 percent said they don’t know or have no opinion. title: Shaheen, DiLorenzo to appear at UNH candidates forum, open to public - seacoastonline.com
content: DURHAM — Republican Anthony DiLorenzo and Democrat Stefany Shaheen are scheduled to appear in a 2026 election candidate forum hosted by the Carsey School of Public Policy at the University of New Hampshire. DiLorenzo and Shaheen, the candidates for the U.S. House in New Hampshire's 1st District, will appear Monday, Oct. 5 from 6 to 7:30 p.m. in the Memorial Union Building at 83 Main St. in Durham. Democratic incumbent Rep. Maggie Goodlander and Republican challenger Lily Tang Williams are scheduled to appear Wednesday, Oct. 7, also from 6 to 7:30 p.m. at the UNH Franklin Pierce School of Law’s Rudman Center, 2 White St., in Concord. Each forum is free and open to the public. The public is required to register in advance at https://carsey.unh.edu/news-events/2026-candidate-policy-forum. UNH faculty, staff, and students will be admitted with a UNH ID. The forums will feature a facilitated 35-minute conversation with each candidate, moderated by Pulitzer-prize journalist Kevin Sullivan, in addition to vetted audience questions. Candidates will be asked to discuss critical issues facing New Hampshire and the nation and explore how international challenges impact the state’s overall well-being. The events are presented in partnership with the Warren B. Rudman Center for Justice, Leadership, & Public Service at UNH's Franklin Pierce School of Law. “New Hampshire voters deserve to understand where their candidates stand on the issues affecting their communities,” said Stephen Bird, director of the Carsey School of Public Policy. “This forum makes that possible.”

David Hobbs, a former Hampton police chief with 27 years of municipal and campus policing experience, joined the University of New Hampshire as its new police chief on Monday. The search for a new police chief followed the resignation of former UNH Police Chief Steven Lee in April, two months after he was arrested for driving under the influence. Since Lee’s arrest, Mark Collopy had served as interim chief. Hobbs most recently served as chief of police and director of public safety at Northern Essex Community College in Massachusetts. There, he expanded community safety programs and worked with student affairs, athletics and Title IX staff on campus safety issues. “I’ve found that the best policing starts with relationships, and that’s especially true at a university,” Hobbs said in a university news release. “I’m looking forward to getting to know UNH students, faculty, and staff and making sure our officers are visible, approachable and prepared.” Dean of Students and Chair of the Search Committee Michael Blackman said two major priorities for filling the role were finding someone with both leadership experience and a background of working with college students. title: Can Surplus-Food Apps Have Too Much Competition? - University of New Hampshire
content: Apps that let businesses sell surplus food at a discount in “surplus bags” have become a popular way to keep edible food out of landfills while giving consumers access to lower-cost meals and groceries. But new research from Wei Wei, assistant professor of decision sciences at UNH's Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics, suggests the results aren't always so straightforward. While surplus-food platforms can benefit businesses, consumers, and the environment, the researchers found that when competition becomes too intense, food waste can rise and retailer profits can fall. One reason: getting surplus food out of a store doesn't necessarily mean it all gets eaten. If consumers receive more food than they need, the extra can still end up wasted at home. In a study published in Decision Sciences, Wei and co-author Zhangchen Hu, assistant professor at California State University, Fullerton, built a mathematical model of how retailers balance traditional in-store sales with sales of discounted surplus bags through apps such as Too Good To Go. Their analysis suggests that while the platforms can create significant benefits, those benefits depend heavily on local market conditions. "The app itself is helping, but what we're really investigating is whether it's always helping in the way it's intended," Wei says. "The result is not automatic. Under certain scenarios, competition can benefit consumers, retailers, and society, but under others, more competition may not be a good thing." Too Good To Go launched in the U.S. in late 2020 and is now used nationwide. As Wei and Hu explored the platform's challenges, they spoke with participating retailers. "I went down to Boston and interviewed a few retailers that participate in the app. They told me it helped them clear out edible food that otherwise might have been thrown away or composted," Wei says. "But a grocery store manager in Cambridge told me participating can also be challenging.  With perishable foods such as prepared foods, baked goods and produce, they don't know how much they'll have left at the end of the day. They have to decide how many surplus bags to make available on the app before they know what their in-store demand will be." Make too many surplus bags available, and retailers risk missing higher-margin in-store purchases. Make too few available, and they may miss the chance to recover value from food that would otherwise go unsold. Pricing adds another wrinkle. Under the platform’s rules, a bag's price is tied to the value of the food inside, so a higher-priced bag is required to contain food with a higher total value. In many cases, that also means more food in the bag. For example, if a bag's price can be no more than 40% of the food's value, a $4 bag would contain at least $10 worth of food. That may suit consumers who need more food but leave others with more than they can use. Competition further complicates those decisions. With more businesses offering surplus bags to the same pool of customers, retailers must decide how to price their bags and how much food to set aside while also accounting for what other participating businesses are doing. "I would expect competition to always help," Wei says. "At first, as competition increases, food waste goes down. But there's a point where that changes. When competition becomes too intense, food waste starts to increase." Consumers continue to benefit as competition increases, but retailers don't share in those gains. The model found that retailer profits decline as more businesses compete on the platform. Wei says the findings aren't an argument against surplus-food platforms. Researchers found many situations where competition among retailers produces a "win-win-win"— higher consumer benefits, higher retailer profits, and lower food waste. In the model, this can occur when surplus bags are offered at a substantial discount and consumers strongly value the bags. The key is understanding the market. A bakery that's one of a dozen on the app in its neighborhood faces very different conditions than one with few nearby competitors, and the model suggests the right pricing and bag-size decisions can differ sharply between the two. "Retailers should not view these platforms as an automatic solution for their surplus food," Wei says. "They need to think strategically about pricing and bag size, while considering their projected in-store demand, how much food their customers actually need and how many other retailers are competing nearby." The platforms themselves can play a role, too. The model suggests that adjusting discount levels based on market conditions could help reduce food waste and, in some cases, improve retailer profits. Helping consumers better understand the value of surplus bags could also improve outcomes. Wei says future research could examine the platform's decisions more directly and how it can balance the interests of businesses, consumers, and food waste reduction. "Overall, their intention is good, and what they are doing is good," Wei says. "The question is how much good they can do and whether they can achieve the best outcome." content: Cloudy. Low 56F. Winds light and variable.. Gov. Kelly Ayotte is pictured at left and Cinde Warmington at right. CONCORD, N.H. — Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s job approval remains above water with New Hampshire voters, but her once-comfortable advantage in the race for governor has narrowed sharply as Democrat Cinde Warmington consolidates support heading into November. A new University of New Hampshire Granite State Poll finds 47% of likely voters supporting Republican Ayotte and 43% supporting Warmington, with Libertarian Stephen Villee at 2%, another candidate at 1% and 7% undecided. The four-point difference is within the poll’s margin of sampling error, leading the UNH Survey Center to characterize the gubernatorial contest as a statistical tie. Just a month ago, Ayotte held a 10-point advantage, 49% to 39%. The movement is particularly notable because it has occurred without any corresponding decline in how New Hampshire residents view Ayotte’s performance as governor. Fifty-one percent approve of the job Ayotte is doing while 44% disapprove, giving her a net approval rating of plus 7 — exactly where it stood in August. Eighty-nine percent of Republicans and 54% of independents approve of her performance, compared with 12% of Democrats. That leaves an unusual split between Ayotte’s job-performance numbers and her standing against Warmington. A majority approves of the governor’s performance, but fewer than half of likely voters currently say they would vote to give her another term. The poll also suggests Warmington’s gain has not been driven by a surge in her personal popularity. Only 18% of likely voters have a favorable opinion of the former Executive Councilor, while 45% view her unfavorably. Another 17% are neutral and 20% say they don’t know enough about her to have an opinion. Ayotte, by comparison, is viewed favorably by 43% of likely voters and unfavorably by 39%, with 16% neutral and just 2% saying they don’t know enough about her. That gives Ayotte a net favorability rating of plus 4, compared with Warmington’s minus 27. Despite that sizable difference in the candidates’ personal ratings, only four percentage points separate them on the ballot test. Partisan voters have largely fallen into line behind their nominees, although Republicans are somewhat more unified behind Ayotte than Democrats are behind Warmington. Ninety-three percent of Republicans support Ayotte, while 84% of Democrats support Warmington. Ayotte also retains a substantial advantage among independents, with 51% supporting her compared with 30% for Warmington. The September result continues a gubernatorial race that has moved considerably during the year. Ayotte led Warmington 47% to 39% in April. Her support fell to 44% in June while Warmington remained at 39%, before Ayotte climbed to 49% in August and opened the race’s largest lead of the year. In the latest survey, Ayotte slipped two points to 47%, while Warmington gained four points to 43%. The undecided share fell from 9% in August to 7% in September. There are signs elsewhere in the poll of a difficult political environment for Republicans. Asked which party’s candidates they would support for the state Senate, 51% of likely voters chose Democrats and 41% Republicans. Democrats also held a 49%-39% advantage on the generic Executive Council ballot and a 49%-39% advantage for the State House. The survey also found widespread dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump’s handling of the trade dispute with Canada. Seventy-one percent of Granite Staters disapprove of his handling of the negotiations, compared with 24% who approve. Among independents, 87% disapprove. Nearly three-quarters of residents — 73% — also said they are concerned about the effect of the trade dispute on New Hampshire, including 88% of independents. The Granite State Poll was conducted online Sept. 17-21 among 1,542 New Hampshire residents. The gubernatorial ballot test is based on likely general election voters. Arbutus Biopharma (ABUS) stock rose 6% on Thursday after the company announced new international patent lawsuits, receipt of a large settlement payment from Moderna and plans to return up to $230 million to shareholders. The stock is now on track for its best day since May 2026 after five consecutive days of trading in the red. On July 8, Arbutus received around $178 million from Moderna, the company said. This represents its share of the payment under the March 2026 global settlement that resolved all patent litigation over Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccines. In March, Arbutus and its partner Genevant Sciences, a unit of Roivant Sciences (ROIV), reached a global settlement with Moderna worth up to $2.25 billion to resolve a long-running dispute over technology used in Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccines. Under the agreement, Moderna is required to make a $950 million upfront payment to both parties, and the payout on July 8 was part of it. The remaining will be paid to Genevant under the settlement agreement. The Moderna patent litigation centered on whether Moderna had used Arbutus’s patented technology without permission in its COVID-19 vaccine. At its core, the dispute was over lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), the tiny fat particles that protect and deliver mRNA into human cells. Without effective LNPs, mRNA vaccines like Moderna’s covid vaccine Spikevax would not work well. Arbutus had developed and patented specific LNP formulations years before the pandemic. Arbutus now expects a dividend from Roivant in the third quarter, owing to its stake in the Genevant parent. Arbutus said it expects to begin returning up to about $230 million to shareholders through share repurchases starting in the third quarter. The buybacks may take the form of a tender offer, open-market purchases, or other methods and will follow receipt of the expected Genevant dividend. However, there is no assurance of the share repurchase activity, the company noted. Following the successful payout from Moderna, Arbutus and Genevant also filed three lawsuits against Pfizer Inc., BioNTech SE and certain of their affiliates to enforce patents covering lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology used in their mRNA COVID-19 vaccines. Cases were lodged in Canada’s Federal Court and two proceedings at the Unified Patent Court in Europe. The company seeks damages and injunctions against Pfizer/BioNTech’s vaccines and any future infringing products. These actions expand an ongoing U.S. patent case in New Jersey. For years, the race to build better artificial intelligence centered on making models bigger, feeding them more data, and expanding the amount of information they could process at once. Now, a fresh frontier is emerging as researchers increasingly explore smarter memory management as another way to build more capable AI systems. Two academic papers published this month, AutoMem and SelfMem, argue that memory shouldn't be a rigid feature engineered by developers using static rules. Instead, they propose that AI systems can learn to manage their own memories. They take different approaches: AutoMem trains AI to manage an external memory system, while SelfMem lets agents refine their own memory strategies through feedback, and both report substantial gains on long-horizon benchmarks. Imagine working with an AI coding assistant on a project for months. Instead of repeatedly reminding it about your project's architecture and coding style, a smarter memory system could retain the decisions that matter while discarding obsolete information. Researchers believe that this kind of selective memory will become increasingly important as AI agents take on longer-running tasks. One way developers have tried to build more capable chatbots is by expanding their context windows, which are the immediate digital scratchpad an AI considers during a conversation. While larger context windows let models process more information, they also increase computational costs and don't necessarily help AI distinguish useful information from irrelevant details. The papers instead explore an alternative approach based on active memory curation. In AutoMem, Stanford University researchers introduced a memory manager that decides when to create, update, search, and delete records, allowing the AI to maintain a compact memory instead of continuously accumulating information. Tested on grueling, complex video games like NetHack and Crafter, this memory-management approach slashed the agent's memory growth rate by 95% and doubled its task performance, allowing a 32-billion-parameter open-weight model to perform competitively with frontier models including Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Thinking on the evaluated long-horizon benchmarks. SelfMem takes a completely parameter-free approach. Instead of editing model weights, it gives the AI a dedicated workspace and tools to inspect an unchangeable transcript store. It allows the agent to inspect, write, review, and revise its own memory, outperforming traditional retrieval pipelines by more than 40% on the BEAM benchmark while using only a fraction of the computational cost. The push for smarter memory comes as AI companies shift from one-off chatbots to autonomous agents designed to work over days or weeks. Whether writing software, tracking supply chains, or managing research projects, these systems must retain relevant information while discarding details that no longer matter. That is where autonomous memory management changes the equation. Instead of forcing a user to repeatedly copy-paste instructions, an agent equipped with an optimized memory workflow seamlessly recalls structural boundaries, tracks cumulative progress, and discards transient data that is no longer relevant. Better memory could also reduce the computational cost of repeatedly processing the same information, a potential advantage as AI companies look to deploy agents more efficiently at scale. Over the past year, leading AI companies like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic have introduced basic memory features, allowing consumer chatbots to retain user preferences and custom instructions across distinct chat sessions. Today's commercial memory features generally rely on predefined mechanisms for deciding what information is retained. AutoMem and SelfMem instead point toward AI systems capable of independently evaluating and regulating their own memories. As tech companies race to build AI systems capable of executing truly long-horizon work, the findings suggest memory management may become an increasingly important complement to larger models. Future AI systems may be judged not only by how much they know, but also by how effectively they decide what information is worth keeping. Lucid Motors (LCID) shares rose for a second straight day on Thursday after the electric vehicle maker forcefully rejected reports that it was considering bankruptcy or a take-private transaction, rebounding from a brutal selloff earlier in the week. The stock traded 12% higher at the time of writing and is on track to clock its best week since July 2025, thanks to a 29% jump on Wednesday, if gains hold. The stock’s dramatic rise and fall started after an Electric-Vehicles.com report on Tuesday said that restructuring adviser AlixPartners has outlined scenarios to the company’s board, including taking the company private or seeking Chapter 11 protection. The stock fell as much as 50% on the news, but pared gains after the company refuted the report as “completely false.” “The company has sufficient liquidity to carry its operations well into next year, as recently published in its last quarterly filings, and it has not formed any special Board committee to explore the scenarios reported today,” Lucid said in a statement to Stocktwits. It also added that AlixPartners is only assisting the company to improve operational performance and did not advise Lucid on a take-private transaction or bankruptcy. They further didn't suggest either option to the company management or board, it added. The company also delivered a cease and desist letter to the publication stating that the company “unequivocally denies the central factual assertions” in the article. Lucid’s new CEO, Silvio Napoli, also said in a post on LinkedIn that the claims circulated were “far from the facts” and that he looks forward to providing a full update on its quarterly earnings call on August 4. Lucid, majority-owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), has faced significant headwinds as an electric vehicle maker. Earlier this month, the company reported second-quarter production of 4,774 vehicles and deliveries of 3,953 units— marking a modest year-over-year increase but short of analyst expectations amid slower-than-hoped demand for the new Gravity SUV. The results coincided with a sweeping leadership overhaul under CEO Silvio Napoli, who assumed the role in June. Napoli replaced CFO Taoufiq Boussaid with automotive finance veteran Alexander De Bock, appointed new executives for technology, customer, digital, and transformation roles, flattened the reporting structure by halving direct reports to the CEO, and eliminated the COO position. These moves followed June layoffs of roughly 1,500 employees, about 18% of the workforce, and the removal of a second production shift at the Arizona plant, aimed at delivering roughly $158 million in annual savings. Financially, Lucid continues to face steep losses and negative gross margins despite revenue growth. In the first quarter, it posted revenue of $282.5 million, up 20% year-over-year, but recorded a net loss of approximately $1.03 billion. The company has relied heavily on its majority shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, for support. It raised about $1.05 billion in April, including $550 million in preferred stock from PIF, $200 million from Uber, and a public offering, and drew an additional $800 million from an existing delayed-draw term loan facility in early July.
